newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Westinghouse industry chief sees growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Westinghouse industry chief sees growth.

text.p: The head of Westinghouse Electric Corp's industrial operations said those struggling units can achieve annual double-digit profit growth through an "ambitious but achievable" business plan he has on the table.

"Personally I'm looking forward to the challenge," Fran Harvey, chief operating officer of Westinghouse's industry and technology group, said Thursday in an interview with Reuters. "We hope to look back with pride and say hey, we restored the corporation to a level of performance it had a long time ago."

The Pittsburgh conglomerate said Wednesday it would split into two separate companies. The industrial company, to be called Westinghouse Electric Co (WELCO), will be based in Pittsburgh. The media company will be based in New York.

WELCO will consist of four business units: power generation, energy systems, government operations and Thermo King, the single industrial gem, which has consistently posted double-digit profit growth.
Harvey, a 28-year Westinghouse veteran, doesn't share Wall Street's view that some of the company's industrial businesses face a lackluster future.

The 52-year-old executive said Westinghouse had no plans to sell any of the units, as analysts have speculated in recent months. "Why would we go through all the trouble of separating if that were going to be the case?" he said. "That alternative was considered and rejected because it's not the optimum solution."
Instead, Harvey said Westinghouse was pursuing a plan of "profitable growth" to strengthen the struggling units, primarily power generation and energy systems.
"We're attacking the cost structure and doing a lot of global sourcing," he said. "I think we're being very proactive in getting the right cost structure to be growing the business."
For energy systems, there is the possibility of "dramatic improvement" through a growing market in China, where Westinghouse is already developing a joint-venture nuclear plant, he said.

"The Chinese have made the decision to make nuclear power a key component of their energy future," he said. "We are jointly developing a next-generation nuclear plant with them." He declined to elaborate, citing competitive reasons.

Harvey said the businesses could grow to the point where the company would eventually need to hire more employees. Westinghouse said in its split announcement that it would lay off 1,100 employees from its industrial operations.
"If we make our ambitious but achievable financial plans a reality, we will be increasing the workforce. No question about it."

Wall Street also has speculated about who Westinghouse Chairman Michael Jordan would put in charge of WELCO. Some analysts said Jordan will hire an outsider who is widely recognized in the business community.
That speculation leaves Harvey unfazed. He said the appointment was the board's decision, and he was going to forge ahead in restoring the company's profitability.
"I'm certainly a candidate for the job," Harvey said. "But in the meantime, we have a job to do and we're going to do it."
